text: Equatorial surface speed of Earth's rotation is about 1,670 km/h
as_written: about 1,670 kilometres per hour
source: IERS sidereal day (23h 56m 4s) and WGS84 equatorial circumference of about 40,075 km, NGA/NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Speed of sound at sea level in the standard atmosphere is about 1,225 km/h (340 m/s)
as_written: about 1,225 kilometres per hour at sea level
source: ISO 2533 / ICAO International Standard Atmosphere

text: Doubling the equatorial speed gives about 3,340 km/h, about 2.7 times the speed of sound
as_written: about 3,340 kilometres per hour, more than two and a half times the speed of sound
source: Derived from 1,670 km/h (IERS, WGS84) and ISO 2533 speed of sound

text: Sun rises and sets in about six hours and night lasts six hours on a 12-hour day at the equator
as_written: the sun climbs and sets in about six hours, and the night is over in six more
source: Derived from a 12-hour rotation period; equatorial day and night are equal at the equinoxes (US Naval Observatory)

text: Earth's rotational kinetic energy is about 2 x 10^29 joules
as_written: roughly two hundred thousand trillion trillion joules
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet moment-of-inertia coefficient 0.3307, Earth mass and radius, IERS rotation rate

text: Rotational energy scales with the square of spin rate, so doubling quadruples it and requires adding three times the current energy
as_written: Double the spin and that figure quadruples, so you would need to add three times as much again
source: Classical mechanics, E = 1/2 I omega^2

text: The added energy (about 6.4 x 10^29 J) equals roughly half an hour of the Sun's total luminosity of 3.828 x 10^26 W
as_written: about half an hour of the entire output of the Sun
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal solar luminosity; derived

text: Centrifugal acceleration at the equator is about 1/289 of gravity
as_written: about one part in 289 of your weight
source: Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy (1967); WGS84 constants

text: Centrifugal effect is a little over a third of one percent of weight today
as_written: a little over a third of one percent
source: Derived from 1/289, Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy

text: Centrifugal effect scales with the square of spin, giving about 1/72, about 1.4 percent, at double spin
as_written: to about one part in 72, which is a bit under one and a half percent
source: Derived from 1/289 times four; Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy

text: Equatorial weight would drop by roughly one percent relative to today
as_written: you would weigh roughly one percent less than you do now
source: Derived: (4 - 1)/289, about 1.0 percent

text: Normal gravity is 9.78 m/s^2 at the equator and 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles
as_written: 9.78 metres per second squared, against 9.83 at the poles
source: WGS84 normal gravity, US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency

text: Equatorial radius is about 6,378 km and polar radius about 6,357 km
as_written: about 6,378 kilometres, and at the poles about 6,357
source: WGS84 ellipsoid, US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency

text: Equatorial radius exceeds polar radius by about 21 km
as_written: roughly 21 kilometres further from the centre
source: WGS84 ellipsoid (6,378.137 km minus 6,356.752 km)

text: To first order the rotational bulge scales with the square of the spin rate, giving a bulge about four times larger, on the order of 80 km
as_written: about four times bigger. That is on the order of eighty kilometres
source: Clairaut's theory of the figure of the Earth, Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy (first-order estimate)

text: With the old sea floor held fixed, the new equilibrium sea surface would be kilometres higher at the equator and kilometres lower near the poles
as_written: kilometres higher than today at the equator, and kilometres lower than today near the poles
source: First-order centrifugal potential calculation, Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy (author's estimate, not a published simulation)

text: Average ocean depth is about 3,700 m
as_written: about 3,700 metres deep
source: Charette and Smith 2010, Oceanography 23(2), ETOPO1-based; NOAA NCEI

text: The Coriolis effect doubles when spin doubles and turns moving water to the right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern
as_written: the sideways push doubles with it
source: Coriolis parameter f = 2 Omega sin(latitude); Gill, Atmosphere-Ocean Dynamics (1982)

text: Geostrophic balance lets ocean currents flow along a sea surface slope
as_written: Oceanographers call this geostrophic balance
source: Gill, Atmosphere-Ocean Dynamics (1982); Rossby 1938 on geostrophic adjustment

text: The Bering Strait is shallow and was dry land during the last ice age, joining Asia and North America
as_written: as they were during the last ice age
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration and USGS, Beringia land bridge

text: Earth's sidereal rotation period is 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds
as_written: 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds
source: International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS)

text: The tropical year is about 365.24 days, so about 731 days of 12 hours
as_written: about 365 and a quarter of today's days. That works out to roughly 731
source: IERS; derived (365.24 sidereal-adjusted days doubled)

text: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4 degrees
as_written: about 23.4 degrees
source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet / IAU obliquity of the ecliptic

text: With a 12-hour rotation, the interval between lunar tides would be about six hours instead of about 12 hours 25 minutes
as_written: roughly every six hours instead of every twelve and a bit
source: Derived from the sidereal month of 27.32 days (NASA Moon Fact Sheet) and a 11h 58m rotation period

text: Human circadian period averages about 24.18 hours
as_written: about 24 and a fifth hours
source: Czeisler et al. 1999, Science 284, 2177-2181

text: Volunteers on 28-hour artificial days did not entrain their body clocks
as_written: such as 28 hours, their body clocks did not follow
source: Czeisler et al. 1999, Science 284, 2177-2181 (forced desynchrony protocol)

text: Arabidopsis grew and survived better when its clock period matched the light-dark cycle
as_written: grew better and survived better when the period of its internal clock matched the cycle of light and dark
source: Dodd et al. 2005, Science 309, 630-633

text: Tropical cyclones do not form within about five degrees of the equator because the Coriolis force is too weak
as_written: within about five degrees of the equator
source: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory, Hurricane Research Division FAQ

text: Because the Coriolis parameter doubles, the same threshold is reached at roughly half the latitude, about 2.5 degrees
as_written: about two and a half degrees
source: Derived from f = 2 Omega sin(latitude)

text: Today's Hadley circulation reaches about 30 degrees latitude, which is where the subtropical deserts lie
as_written: toward about 30 degrees of latitude
source: NOAA / NASA climate education on Hadley circulation and subtropical deserts

text: Climate model experiments show faster rotation gives narrower Hadley cells and more jets
as_written: The faster the spin, the narrower the tropical overturning cell
source: Navarra and Boccaletti 2002, Climate Dynamics 19; Kaspi and Showman 2015, Astrophysical Journal 804

text: Navarra and Boccaletti study of rotation-rate sensitivity was published in 2002
as_written: Navarra and Boccaletti in 2002
source: Navarra and Boccaletti 2002, Climate Dynamics 19, 467-481

text: Eastward equatorial launches gain about 465 m/s from Earth's rotation
as_written: about 465 metres per second
source: NASA; derived from equatorial rotation speed

text: Low Earth orbit requires about 7.8 km/s
as_written: about 7.8 kilometres per second
source: NASA orbital velocity reference

text: 465 m/s is about six percent of 7.8 km/s
as_written: about six percent of the job
source: Derived

text: Doubling gives about 930 m/s, nearly twelve percent of orbital speed
as_written: about 930 metres per second, nearly twelve percent
source: Derived

text: The 1960 Chile earthquake was magnitude 9.5, the largest recorded
as_written: magnitude 9.5
source: United States Geological Survey, Largest Earthquakes in the World

text: The 1960 Chile earthquake occurred in 1960
as_written: in Chile in 1960
source: United States Geological Survey

text: Postglacial rebound continues in Scandinavia and Canada thousands of years after ice sheet melt, showing the mantle relaxes over thousands of years
as_written: thousands of years after their ice sheets melted
source: Peltier 2004, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 32; Fennoscandian and Laurentide rebound studies

text: At double spin the equatorial bulge is about four times today's
as_written: an equator nearly four times as swollen as now
source: Clairaut's theory, Heiskanen and Moritz, Physical Geodesy (first-order)

text: Christensen and Aubert 2006 found dynamo field strength in fast-rotating regimes depends on heat flux, not directly on rotation rate
as_written: A well-known scaling study by Christensen and Aubert in 2006
source: Christensen and Aubert 2006, Geophysical Journal International 166, 97-114

text: Tidal friction lengthens the day by about two milliseconds per century
as_written: about two milliseconds per century
source: Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 472

text: The Moon recedes at about 3.8 cm per year, measured by lunar laser ranging off Apollo reflectors
as_written: about 3.8 centimetres every year
source: NASA Apollo lunar laser ranging retroreflector experiment; Dickey et al. 1994, Science 265

text: At 2 ms per century, adding 12 hours would take about 2.2 billion years
as_written: more than two billion years
source: Derived: 43,200 s divided by 2 ms per century

text: Devonian corals about 400 million years ago show roughly 400 days per year, implying a day of about 22 hours
as_written: about 400 million years ago record daily growth lines, and the lines per year add up to roughly 400 days, which means a day of about 22 hours
source: Wells 1963, Nature 197, 948-950

text: Wells published in 1963
as_written: John Wells in 1963
source: Wells 1963, Nature 197, 948-950

text: Some models of the Moon-forming impact give the young Earth a day of only a few hours, a topic still debated
as_written: a day of only a few hours
source: Cuk and Stewart 2012, Science 338, 1047-1052; Canup 2012, Science 338, 1052-1055

text: Geostationary orbit altitude is 35,786 km and the period is one sidereal day
as_written: 35,786 kilometres above the equator
source: NASA; International Telecommunication Union

text: A geostationary satellite completes one orbit in about 24 hours
as_written: about 24 hours
source: NASA; sidereal day of 23h 56m (IERS)

text: A satellite with half the orbital period would be at an altitude of about 20,200 km (orbital radius scales with period to the two-thirds power)
as_written: to about 20,200 kilometres
source: Kepler's third law; GPS Interface Specification IS-GPS-200 (orbital radius about 26,560 km)

text: GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km altitude
as_written: the altitude of the GPS satellites
source: GPS.gov, US Space Force; IS-GPS-200

text: GPS satellites orbit about twice per sidereal day with a period of about 11 hours 58 minutes
as_written: about 11 hours and 58 minutes
source: GPS.gov; IS-GPS-200

text: Relative to a rotating ground, a satellite with a 24-hour period would move westward at about 15 degrees per hour
as_written: about 15 degrees every hour
source: Derived: 360 degrees per sidereal day is 15.04 degrees per hour; kinematic difference of 2 rev and 1 rev per sidereal day

text: GPS orbits are inclined about 55 degrees to the equator
as_written: tilted about 55 degrees
source: GPS.gov; IS-GPS-200

text: The equator would stay on the surface unless Earth spun about 17 times faster, giving an orbital period at the surface of about 84 minutes
as_written: about 84 minutes, which is a spin about seventeen times faster than today
source: Derived from WGS84 GM and equatorial radius (low circular orbit period about 84 minutes); IERS rotation period
